pl-l2d35c1-d1e111.summary: Gives Augustine's definition: sin is every word, deed, or desire against the law of God.

pl-l2d35c1-d1e114.summary: Gives Augustine's definition in De duabus animabus: sin is the will to keep or obtain what justice forbids.
claims: Sin is a will contrary to justice.

pl-l2d35c1-d1e118.summary: Explains that both concern actual mortal sin, not venial; the first makes sin an evil will or evil speech and deed, interior and exterior act; the second only an interior act, since will is a motion of the mind.
claims: One includes exterior acts; the other only interior.

pl-l2d35c1-d1e121.summary: Cites Ambrose, De paradiso: sin is transgression of divine law and disobedience to heavenly commands; sin is in the transgressor, not in the one commanding; without prohibition there would be no sin, and without sin perhaps no virtue, which could neither subsist nor stand out without seeds of malice.
claims: Virtue may require the possibility of malice.

pl-l2d35c1-d1e129.summary: Notes that Ambrose defines sin as transgression of law and disobedience.

pl-l2d35c1.summary: Asks what sin is. Augustine: sin is every word, deed, or desire against the law of God; and sin is the will to keep or obtain what justice forbids. Both concern actual mortal sin, not venial; the first makes sin evil will or evil speech and deed, interior and exterior acts; the second only an interior act, will being a motion of the mind. Ambrose: sin is transgression of the divine law and disobedience to heavenly commands; without prohibition there would be no sin, and perhaps no virtue.
claims: Sin is every word, deed, or desire against God's law.
Sin is the will to keep or obtain what justice forbids.
These definitions concern actual mortal sin.
Ambrose defines sin as transgression of divine law and disobedience.
Without prohibition there would be no sin.
